activities.title: Count and read word parts
materials: words: sunset, picnic, napkin, rabbit, basket, pencil, cactus
parentPrompts: Explain: "Every part of a word, called a syllable, has a vowel sound." Clap the parts of your child's name, then "picnic" (pic-nic).
Write picnic on a card and draw a line between the parts: pic | nic. Read each part, then the whole word.
Do the same with sunset, napkin, rabbit, basket. Have your child cover half the word with a finger to read one part at a time.
Ask: "How many claps? How many vowel sounds do you hear?" They should match.
Check: your child reads at least four of the words by splitting into parts and can tell you how many parts each has.

activities.title: Add endings to base words
materials: base words: jump, look, help, play, walk
parentPrompts: Write "jump" and read it. Add -s, -ed, and -ing on separate cards and read jumps, jumped, jumping. Ask: "Which one means it is happening now? Which one means it already happened?"
Use the endings with look, help, play, and walk. Read each new word aloud.
Act them out: "Show me jumping. Show me you walked." Then say a sentence for your child to finish: "Yesterday I ___."
Have your child write one word with each ending in a short sentence.
Check: your child reads the endings correctly and can tell now from past with at least three words.

activities.title: Write about something that happened
materials: three sheets of paper or one folded in three
parentPrompts: Pick something real that happened, such as a trip to the park or baking something together. Talk it through: "What happened first? What happened next? What happened last?"
Have your child draw three pictures in order and write one sentence under each, using the words First, Next, and Last.
Ask: "How did you feel? What did you see or hear?" Have your child add one detail to a sentence.
Read it together and add an end mark and a capital letter where needed.
Check: three events appear in the right order with the words first, next, last, and at least one added detail.

activities.title: Write an animal fact page
materials: a library book or two about an animal your child likes
parentPrompts: Pick an animal. Look through the book together and find three facts. Ask: "What does it eat? Where does it live? What is its body like?"
Have your child say each fact in a full sentence before writing: "A frog lives near water."
Write the topic at the top, then three fact sentences. Draw and label a picture.
Finish with a closing sentence, such as "Frogs are cool."
Check: a topic, at least two true facts from the book, and a closing sentence. Ask your child where they found each fact.

activities.title: Read your writing to an audience
materials: your child's writing from this week
a stuffed animal or family member as audience
parentPrompts: Have your child pick their favorite piece from this month and read it aloud, pointing to each word.
Teach the listener to ask a question: "Can you tell me more about ...?" Your child answers and adds a detail to the writing.
Ask: "What is one thing you did well? What would you like to work on next?"
Celebrate: save the piece in a folder for the end of the unit.
Check: your child reads clearly with their finger under the words, answers a question about it in a full sentence, and adds one detail.

activities.title: Bundle straws into tens
materials: 30 or more craft sticks or straws
parentPrompts: Count out 23 straws. Ask: "How can we count faster?" Show how to bundle ten at a time with a rubber band.
Ask: "How many bundles of ten? How many extra ones? So 23 is 2 tens and 3 ones."
Say a number like 14, 31 or 20 and have your child build it with bundles and single straws. Notice that 20 has two tens and no ones.
Write the number and circle the tens digit in one color and the ones digit in another.
Check: your child builds three numbers correctly and says "tens" and "ones" for each. Safety: keep rubber bands away from faces and pets.

activities.title: Show numbers on a tens and ones chart
materials: paper with two columns labeled Tens and Ones
bundles and single straws from the last lesson
parentPrompts: Put the paper in front of your child. Place 3 bundles in Tens and 6 singles in Ones. Ask: "What number is this?" (36).
Write 36 under the columns. Ask: "Which digit tells how many tens?"
Call out 52, 47, 80 and 61. Your child builds each and writes the number.
Show a built number and have your child write it. Ask about a trick: "Is 63 the same as 36? Why not?"
Check: your child builds and writes four numbers correctly and tells you what each digit stands for.

activities.title: Compare two-digit numbers
parentPrompts: Build 34 and 28 with straws. Ask: "Which has more tens? Which number is bigger?"
Introduce the symbols: the open mouth faces the bigger number. Write 34 > 28 and 28 < 34. Say them aloud.
Flip two number cards and compare them. Ask: "What do you look at first, the tens or the ones?"
Play five rounds. For equal numbers, use =.
Check: your child compares at least four pairs correctly and explains that they look at the tens first.

activities.title: Measure objects with units
materials: a box of paper clips or small blocks that are all the same size
a few objects to measure (a book, a spoon, a shoe)
parentPrompts: Pick a pencil. Line up paper clips end to end along it with no gaps or overlaps. Count them. Say: "The pencil is 6 paper clips long."
Predict first: "Will the book be longer or shorter than 10 clips?" Measure and check.
Order three objects from shortest to longest and write the clip count under each.
Ask: "What happens if we use bigger units, like blocks? Will the number be larger or smaller?" Try it.
Check: your child lines up units end to end with no gaps and states the length as a number of units. Safety: keep small units away from younger siblings.

activities.title: Make a tally chart and answer questions
materials: 10 to 15 small items in three kinds (e.g., socks, spoons, blocks), or ask family about favorites among three snacks
parentPrompts: Check for food allergies before using any snack food.
Pick three categories, such as favorite fruit: apple, banana, grapes. Ask everyone in the home (or draw a few tallies yourself) and make tally marks.
Count each category and write the number. Ask: "How many in all?"
Ask: "Which has the most? Which has the fewest? How many more apples than grapes?"
Draw a simple picture graph with one square per vote.
Check: your child answers all four questions correctly using the chart or graph.

subject: science
title: Design a shelter like an animal

activities.title: Build a shelter model
materials: paper bags, craft sticks, tape, leaves or fabric scraps
a small toy animal or a paper animal
parentPrompts: Explain: "Engineers sometimes get ideas from nature. Today your job is to make a small shelter that keeps a toy animal dry and safe."
Look at pictures of animal homes (a bird nest, a beehive, a burrow). Ask: "What materials do animals use?"
Plan and build. Ask: "What will your shelter be made of? Why?"
Test: spray lightly with water (or pour a little) and see if the animal stays dry. Ask: "What could you change?"
Check: your child builds, tests, and changes one thing to improve it. They tell what part of an animal or plant gave them an idea.

subject: science
title: Design a tool like a beak or claw

activities.title: Build a gripper
materials: small objects to pick up (cotton balls, pom-poms)
parentPrompts: Review: animals use parts like beaks, claws, and trunks to pick things up. Ask: "Which animal part can you copy?"
Challenge: build a tool that can pick up a cotton ball and move it to a cup. Use clothespins or craft sticks with rubber bands.
Test. Count how many items you can move in one minute. Ask: "What worked? What would you change?"
Make one improvement and test again.
Check: your child says which animal part inspired the tool and explains one change. Safety: keep rubber bands away from faces; supervise small parts.

activities.title: Test a covering
materials: 2 small cups of warm (not hot) water
parentPrompts: Explain: some animals have fur or feathers that keep them warm. Today you will test a "coat."
Wrap one cup of warm tap water with fabric and leave the other cup bare. Make sure the water is only warm, never hot.
Wait ten minutes. Touch both cups or use a thermometer. Ask: "Which stayed warmer? Why might that help an animal?"
Try another material and compare.
Check: your child compares the two cups and says which covering kept the water warmer. Safety: use warm tap water only, not hot.

activities.title: Draw a map of our neighborhood helpers
materials: pictures or memory of places in your neighborhood
parentPrompts: Draw your home in the middle. Ask: "Where is the nearest library, fire station, park, or store?" Add them to the map.
Add a key to the map: a small symbol and a label for each place.
Ask: "Who works at each place? Who helps people there?"
Trace a path from home to one place and tell about it using words like near, far, next to.
Check: your child draws at least three places, adds labels, and describes a route with position words.

activities.title: Plan a way to help
parentPrompts: Ask: "How can you be a helper in our home or neighborhood?" Brainstorm ideas such as setting the table or watering plants.
Choose one and make a plan: "What will I do? When? How will I know I did it?"
Make a thank-you card for a helper you chose (a mail carrier, librarian, or neighbor).
Talk about how it feels to help and to be thanked.
Check: your child plans one way to help and does it this week; they say how it helps others.
